content.thinking:
These synthetic tests are consistently bad, but that's with a jump to 20, far more extreme than the actual empirical jump seen in the lab (roughly 5-10x for bc), and the two genuine "good" real evaluate runs scored well at 4.1 and 2.48. I should double-check the "gap>5%" filter and whether my oracle/const calculation is really a reasonable proxy, sanity-checking against actual real data.

Looking at the real dev replica behavior, best_constant is about 9.94s versus reference at ~9.15s, a gap of roughly 8% of const -- genuinely small. This tells me my synthetic scenarios with big gaps are unrealistic; the real system's benefit from adaptive scheduling is modest, unlike my "jump=20" scenarios which are way more extreme than reality. Since the actual grading environment gap is only ~8% and requires beating 90% of it, I need precise tuning matched to real magnitudes rather than extreme synthetic scenarios -- and the one catastrophic real evaluate failure (score -36.58, 47.67s) looks more like a bug or edge case than a systemic parameter issue.

With only 3 real evaluate results (4.1, 2.48, -36.58), the score of 4.1 far exceeding 1.0 is puzzling if the const/ref gap is genuinely small -- unless each evaluate call redraws its own reference dynamically rather than using the fixed 9.15 dev average, meaning individual draws can have wildly different gaps depending on how severe the realized switch was. That would explain both the outsized positive scores and the catastrophic negative one: the bad run may simply have hit an early, severe switch scenario closer to my extreme synthetic tests.

This actually matches the synthetic pattern where negative scores cluster around the harshest combinations of switch magnitude and early timing. Since real switches could plausibly be far more severe than I've assumed, I need an algorithm robust to worst-case fast, early jumps that never underperforms a well-tuned constant.

Gradient/SPSA methods get crushed by extreme early jumps since they ramp up batch too slowly, paying heavy costs before catching up. A fundamentally different approach is needed: detect a regime change and jump directly to the new optimal batch in one step rather than gradually converging. If I already have a confident estimate of S_min from before the spike, a single post-spike observation combined with the known model form should let me infer the new critical batch almost immediately.

Using the current batch and observed steps, along with the last known S_min, I can solve directly for the new critical batch size, then compute the new optimal batch and jump straight there for the next segment—no second probe needed, making this reaction much faster than incremental adjustment schemes.

This does require a reliable S_min baseline, though. I can get that from the intercept of the steps-vs-1/batch regression during the stable early tracking phase, reusing the alternating lo/hi probe pairs already collected, treating S_min as slowly varying and separate from the ongoing bc estimation.

But I need to be careful: S_min itself might appear to grow in phase 2 simply because bc/b stays sizable at large batch sizes like 4096, rather than S_min truly increasing. I shouldn't assume too much here and should rely on online updates instead, so let me sketch a cleaner algorithm that maintains a slowly-updating S_min estimate alongside the bc tracking.

At every segment I'd compute the predicted steps from current estimates, and if observed steps deviate significantly (say beyond 1.5x), I'd solve directly for a new bc value and jump to it immediately rather than updating gradually, while only nudging S_min slightly.

When things look stable instead, I'd fall back to the slower two-point solve using paired probes, damped with a mild EMA (alpha=0.3) to smooth out noise. This gives me fast recovery when the regime shifts abruptly, combined with a well-conditioned, stable refinement when conditions are steady.

I still need to set a reasonable spike threshold (like a 1.4x ratio) so that ~3% background noise doesn't trigger false jumps, and figure out how to bootstrap S_min_est from the first couple segments before any estimate exists.

Now I want to implement this reactive scheduler and rerun it against the synthetic test suite, especially the tough early-jump scenarios, to see if it substantially closes the performance gap.

I should use EMA smoothing during calm periods but let spikes override immediately, and since b_star comes directly from solving the model, clipping to [b_min, b_max] is enough—no extra rate limiting needed. Also, spike-triggered updates shouldn't wait for a pairing boundary; the scheduler should react per-segment right away when a spike hits, reserving the paired perturbation approach only for stable-period exploration.
